issues.legal_issue: A court exercising constitutional supervisory jurisdiction may make a remand on the occupant’s status conditional on allowing a public body to pursue a previously rejected claim for damages when the occupant’s status and liability for use and occupation are interdependent.
material_facts: The eviction order against the company was challenged, and the appellate court had reversed the damages order because it was unsupported by adequate evidence.
The public body did not challenge the appellate court’s decision on damages.

The High Court set aside the eviction and damages orders as to the company and remanded the matter for a fresh decision on whether its sub-tenancy was lawful, allowing the public body to pursue damages if the company was found to be an unauthorised occupant.
The company remained in possession, and the damages claim depended on whether its occupation was authorised or unauthorised.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to balance the equities by allowing the damages claim to be considered on remand, contingent on a finding that the company was an unauthorised occupant; the Supreme Court declined to interfere.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, the High Court may consider the whole case and make appropriate orders to achieve substantial justice. Its equitable jurisdiction may require a party seeking relief to relinquish an unfair advantage, and a remand may address interdependent questions of occupation and compensation for use and occupation. No earlier case was relied on.

predicates.constitutional_review_of_eviction_procee: A party sought constitutional review of an eviction decision concerning its occupation of premises.
predicates.damages_rejected_for_insufficient_eviden: A prior decision rejected the damages claim because the evidence supporting its assessment was inadequate.
predicates.damages_claim_not_challenged: The party seeking damages did not challenge the prior decision rejecting that claim.
predicates.occupation_status_determines_damages_lia: Whether the occupant is authorised or unauthorised determines whether damages for use and occupation may be claimed.

issues.definition: When constitutional review of an eviction decision involves a damages claim previously rejected for insufficient evidence and not challenged, and damages liability depends on occupation status, the court may allow that claim to be reconsidered on remand subject to the status finding.

issues.legal_issue: Liability for damages for use and occupation of public premises depends on the occupant first being found to be unauthorised.
material_facts: The proceedings concerned eviction from premises treated as public premises and a claim for payment for their use and occupation.
The damages claim depended on whether the company’s sub-tenancy was lawful and whether it was therefore an unauthorised occupant.
issues.conclusion: Damages may be required only if the occupant is found to be unauthorised; an authorised occupant may instead be required to pay rent.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(f), 4, 5 and 7 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 distinguish rent payable by an authorised occupant from damages payable by an unauthorised occupant. The statutory scheme makes the occupant’s status a prerequisite to the corresponding liability; no earlier case was relied on.

predicates.public_premises_occupation_proceeding: Proceedings concern a person's occupation of premises treated as public premises.
predicates.occupant_found_unauthorised: The decision-maker finds that the occupant is not authorised to occupy the premises.

issues.definition: In proceedings about occupation of public premises, a finding that the occupant is unauthorised permits the occupant to be required to pay damages.
